title: Rethinking Joint Maximum Mean Discrepancy for Visual Domain Adaptation

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 (Datasets and Experimental Settings), description of D²
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper describes ImageCLEF-DA as 'a constructed dataset synthesized for this study,' but ImageCLEF-DA is a well-established, pre-existing cross-domain benchmark used by numerous prior works (e.g., the baselines RMMD, RSDA-MSTN, SPL, OGL²P compared against in Table 7 all report results on it independently). Claiming it was synthesized for this study misattributes/mischaracterizes a standard public benchmark.

The reference entry contains an inserted editorial note: '(Note: This reference has been adjusted to reflect the last officially verified publication year.)' This flags that the citation's year/volume/page information was altered or is unverified, which is inappropriate for a published bibliography and suggests a fabricated or inconsistent citation record.

The paper states 'K^1 = I_{n×n} is a matrix whose elements are all 1', but I_{n×n} conventionally denotes the identity matrix (1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere), which contradicts the stated property that all elements equal 1. The appendix (Theorem 5) correctly uses the all-ones notation '1_{n×n}', creating an internal notational/mathematical inconsistency with the main text.

The individual task accuracies listed for OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC (96.1, 95.3, 77.6, 98.1, 77.1, 99.1) average to approximately 90.55, but the table reports an average of 90.1, an internal inconsistency within the table itself.

Table 1 reports OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC average of 90.1 on Office-31, while Table 3 (ablation study on the same dataset/method) reports OGLP+JMMD-HSIC = 91.5 ± 1.3 for Office-31. These two values for the same model/dataset combination directly contradict each other.

The text claims 'OGL²P+JMMD-HSIC achieves the best average results among all compared approaches, with 0.3% and 0.5% improvements over the second-best method, i.e., RSDA-MSTN,' but Table 1 shows OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC average (90.1) is actually lower than RSDA-MSTN (91.2) on Office-31, directly contradicting the claim of being best and the stated 0.3% improvement.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix Section F, comparison of SPL+Our/OGL2P+Our on Office10-Caltech10 (Table 6)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states improvements of '1.5%/0.4%... on the two datasets,' implying OGL2P+Our improves by 0.4% over OGL2P on D¹ (Office10-Caltech10). However, Table 6 shows OGL2P baseline average = 94.6 and OGL2P+Our = 94.3 (or 94.5 by recomputation), both lower than or inconsistent with a +0.4% claimed improvement, indicating a decrease rather than an improvement.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix Section F, concluding paragraph on Table 6/7 results
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'OGL²P+JMMD-HSIC achieves the best average results among all compared approaches, obtaining 0.4% and 0.7% improvements compared with the second-best method, i.e., OGL²P.' For D¹ (Table 6), the OGL2P baseline (94.6) is actually higher than OGL2P+Our (94.3), making OGL2P the best performer, not the 'second-best' surpassed by the proposed method, contradicting the stated conclusion.

The paper admits: 'we set it to 0.5 for JDA+JMMD-HSIC, and performed targeted manual tuning per dataset for the other two variants to maximize performance, with selective reporting of best results.' This describes a form of hyperparameter cherry-picking/selective reporting across different methods, which undermines fair comparison and is a methodological flaw that should be corrected or disclosed with proper validation protocol.

The text acknowledges 'some baseline methods employ alternative pretrained features or fine-tuning strategies, potentially affecting direct comparability' and 'uniformity across comparison baselines is not guaranteed,' yet the paper still presents direct numerical comparisons (e.g., Tables 1, 2, 6, 7) and draws conclusions of superiority without correcting for this acknowledged confound, which is a methodological inconsistency undermining the validity of the comparative claims.
